title: The Painful Truth of Exactly How ICE’s New Shock Gloves Actually Work
gist: A Department of Homeland Security notice reveals ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on 'GLOVE' shock gloves made by Compliant Technologies of Lexington, Kentucky — a pain-compliance device that shocks bare skin at up to 380 V rather than incapacitating like a Taser. The piece details the hardware (rechargeable battery, microprocessor, microSD or internal-memory audit logging), the certification and use restrictions, and a human-rights researcher's argument that the category is inherently abusive.

insights.claim: A Department of Homeland Security notice discloses that ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on electric shock gloves, establishing a concrete near-term federal budget line for non-lethal pain-compliance apparel.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A $20M single-category award is a visible slice of the expanding immigration-enforcement equipment budget; watch DHS notices as a leading indicator of which small private suppliers get scaled.
insights.quote: ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to subdue an individual
insights.locator: With the revelation that ICE will spend

insights.claim: The supplier of ICE's shock gloves is Compliant Technologies, a privately held manufacturer based in Lexington, Kentucky, whose GLOVE product was previously sold into US jails and police departments before this federal-scale order.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific niche vendor whose revenue base shifts from municipal corrections to federal immigration enforcement — the kind of small-cap or private target defense/security roll-ups acquire.
insights.locator: These shock gloves go by the unsubtle acronym of GLOVE

insights.claim: GLOVE units can only be sold to verified professional entities such as the military, correctional facilities, and law enforcement agencies, meaning the manufacturer's addressable market is entirely institutional and procurement-driven with no consumer channel.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Revenue is fully exposed to government budget cycles and policy reversals — high concentration risk alongside high growth if enforcement spending continues.
insights.locator: GLOVE, which can only be sold to verified professional entities

insights.claim: Compliant Technologies did not respond to WIRED's request for comment on its shock-glove product, an opacity signal from a supplier newly exposed to federal-scale scrutiny.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Vendors in politically charged procurement often avoid press; expect reputational risk to be priced only when contracts become public.
insights.locator: Compliant Technologies did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.

themes.theme: CD3 device mechanics versus Taser-class weapons

insights.claim: The GLOVE is classified as a CD3 (conductive distraction and de-escalation device) and works by neuro-peripheral interference — shocking skin to bombard sensory nerves — rather than the neuromuscular incapacitation used by stun guns and Tasers that override the central nervous system.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: CD3 is a distinct regulatory and product category from conducted-energy weapons; regulation or bans on Taser-class devices would not automatically capture it, and vice versa.
insights.quote: the GLOVE works using neuro-peripheral interference, essentially shocking the skin to bombard the sensory nerves and temporarily short-circuit the brain's focus

insights.claim: The GLOVE delivers high-frequency electrical pulses through conductive pads on the palm and finger undersides, powered by a rechargeable battery and microprocessor module in a zippered cuff pouch, activated by a one-second press on a wrist switch.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: The bill of materials is commodity wearable electronics — battery, microcontroller, conductive textiles — implying low manufacturing barriers and likely high gross margin on institutional pricing.
insights.locator: When activated via a one-second press on a wrist switch

insights.claim: Maximum voltage on all GLOVE generations is capped at 380 V, with minimum voltage of 210 V on Gen 3 and 4 rising to 324 V on Gen 5, and maximum continuous stimulation time of two hours on Gen 3/4 falling to 90 minutes on Gen 5.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Generational specs show the product line moving toward a narrower, higher-floor voltage band — a design trend regulators and litigators will scrutinize.
insights.locator: Maximum voltage is capped at 380 V for all

insights.claim: The manufacturer claims the gloves produce subject compliance in under three seconds and leave no burns, marks, or scars, a marketing property that also makes physical evidence of use hard to document after the fact.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Mark-free pain compliance shifts accountability entirely onto device logs and body-worn camera evidence, raising the value of audit-trail and evidence-management vendors.
insights.quote: leave no burns, marks, or scars
insights.locator: The manufacturer claims the gloves result in a subject's compliance

insights.claim: Current flows only between the glove's contact pads and the subject's skin, so the wearing officer and assisting officers holding the subject should not feel shocks — a design property that enables multi-officer restraint scenarios that Taser deployment does not.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Officer-safe operation broadens tactical use cases versus probe weapons, supporting wider unit-per-officer adoption rather than one-per-squad deployment.
insights.locator: Because the current flows only between the contact pads

insights.claim: Gen 4 and Gen 5 GLOVEs record 'activation events' capturing date, hour, minute and skin-contact time for audit trails, with Gen 4 storing data on a removable microSD card and Gen 5 replacing that with internal memory accessed over USB-C.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: The move from removable media to sealed internal memory is a chain-of-custody upgrade that mirrors body-camera evidence norms — a template for how force-device telemetry becomes discoverable data.
insights.quote: tracking the date, hour, minute, and skin-contact time for audit trails and after-action reporting
insights.locator: Gen 4 and 5 of GLOVE both include mechanisms

insights.claim: GLOVE operators must be certified and recertified every other year, and manuals cap continuous shocks at 15 seconds, limit use to one pair per subject, restrict targeting to arms and legs, and exclude the elderly, young children, pregnant individuals and people with severe disabilities.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A dense manufacturer-defined use protocol creates a recurring training/certification revenue stream and a clear negligence standard plaintiffs can measure deployments against.
insights.locator: has some clear usage recommendations in Compliant Technologies' instruction manuals

insights.claim: The GLOVE requires bare-skin contact and will not work through dry clothing or thick hair, though it does function through thin wet clothing such as soaked T-shirts, and is likely rendered inoperable if dunked in water.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: The bare-skin dependency sharply limits field effectiveness in cold-weather or clothed encounters, capping real-world utility relative to the procurement dollars committed.
insights.quote: the gloves won't work through dry clothing or thick hair

insights.claim: The GLOVE's battery is rated for 2,000 charge/discharge cycles with a two-hour full recharge and four LED indicators showing 25 percent increments, and the device operates between 14 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: A 2,000-cycle battery implies a multi-year service life and therefore a replacement-and-consumables cycle rather than recurring hardware revenue in the near term.
insights.locator: The battery is apparently good for 2,000 charge/discharge cycles

themes.theme: Human rights pushback as regulatory risk

insights.claim: Michael Crowley of the Omega Research Foundation argues CD3 devices are inherently abusive because they are designed to influence through pain rather than to restrain or incapacitate, and should not be manufactured, sold or used by law enforcement including ICE.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Organized human-rights opposition to an entire device class is the precursor to export-control or municipal-procurement bans — a tail risk for suppliers concentrated in this category.
insights.quote: The company talks about it as a de-escalation solution, but the whole idea of it is to get control or influence somebody through pain.
insights.locator: Michael Crowley, a senior researcher at Omega Research Foundation

insights.claim: Compliant Technologies' own manuals state the technology must not be used to counter verbal defiance, as punishment, or for torture — an explicit acknowledgment by the manufacturer that the device's failure mode is abuse rather than malfunction.
insights.speaker: Jeremy White
insights.so_what: Manufacturer-documented prohibited uses become the evidentiary backbone of civil-rights litigation once deployment data and logs are subpoenaed.
insights.quote: The technology must not be used to counter verbal defiance, as punishment, or for torture.
insights.locator: The technology must not be used to counter verbal defiance
